title: Permitting reform is likely move for Democratic controlled US Congress
gist: Wood Mackenzie argues that with Democrats winning Congress in the 2026 midterms, permitting reform (via the bipartisan BAAJA) is the likeliest energy-affordability policy, chiefly helping gas power, pipelines, transmission and wind, though vetoes, executive action and state policies create risk. The release gives figures on gas-fired build-out (166 GW), BTM gas demand and transformer deficits. The text mentions both a two-year and one-year NEPA review deadline.

insights.claim: Democrats capturing both the House and Senate in the US midterms could make permitting reform a top agenda item for advancing power growth and cutting energy costs, per Wood Mackenzie.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Policy regime shift raises odds of infrastructure approval acceleration, favoring gas, transmission and wind developers.

insights.claim: Energy costs rose with the conflict in Iran, which pushed peak US diesel and jet fuel prices roughly 2.5 times above pre-war forecasts; the hardest-hit products are still expected to be 30% above pre-war forecasts in 2027 even as prices ease.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Elevated fuel prices persist into 2027, supporting the affordability politics.
insights.locator: The elections came amid rising energy costs

insights.claim: The midterm results signal a sentiment shift in which energy cost has emerged as a check on the president's agenda, creating common ground for both parties on affordability.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Affordability is a bipartisan lever, making cost-reducing energy supply measures more politically viable.
insights.locator: The midterm results point to a sentiment shift

insights.claim: A Democratic Congress does not guarantee legislation under a Republican White House: the president retains veto authority and executive agencies can dilute any law that passes.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Legislative success is far from assured; discount headline policy optimism.
insights.locator: A Democratic Congress does not guarantee

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie base case has US load growth lifted 3% from 2026 to 2035 by data centers and power infrastructure, with wholesale power prices up 46% over the same period, making affordability a key driver for permitting goals.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Rising wholesale prices underpin both political urgency and merchant generation economics.
insights.locator: With rapid development in data centers

themes.theme: Three policy levers and their odds

insights.claim: Congress has three levers for energy affordability with very different odds: permitting reform (likeliest), renewable subsidies (unlikely), and large-load cost rules (left to states).
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Rank-ordering policy odds helps positioning: back permitting beneficiaries over subsidy-dependent plays.

insights.claim: New renewable energy credits are unlikely despite Democratic proposals to expand subsidies because of the expected presidential veto.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Subsidy-dependent renewable business models should not count on new federal credits.

insights.claim: Federal mandates on large-load cost rules face legal and political resistance, so states will set cost allocation policy for data centers.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Data center cost allocation will be a patchwork of state rules, a variable in site selection and power contracts.

insights.claim: Permitting reform is viewed as the likeliest route to faster gas, transmission and wind approvals, with nuclear, CCUS and upstream getting an incremental boost.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gas, grid and wind are the primary beneficiaries; nuclear, CCUS and upstream benefit at the margin.

themes.theme: BAAJA permitting provisions and gas build-out

insights.claim: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), backed by key Senate architects and a coalition of clean energy developers, oil and gas producers, miners and trade unions, could speed infrastructure approvals.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Broad cross-industry coalition improves the bill's odds relative to partisan proposals.

insights.claim: BAAJA key provisions: NEPA environmental analyses completed within two years, no federal revocation of permits, litigation limited to a 150-day window after environmental approval, and a 9-month timeline for water quality dredge and fill permits for new gas pipelines.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Shorter timelines and reduced litigation tail lower project risk and cost of capital for pipelines and generation.
insights.quote: Limits litigation to a 150-day window after project environmental approvals are issued

insights.claim: Permitting reform matters most for front-of-the-meter gas-fired power, which sits away from gas supply basins and needs new pipelines to deliver Wood Mackenzie's forecast of 166 GW net new gas-fired capacity in 2026-2035.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Pipeline permitting is the gating factor for the gas power build-out, favoring midstream developers.
insights.locator: Permitting reform matters most for front-of-the-meter

insights.claim: Behind-the-meter gas demand is approaching 6 bcfd, about 6% of US domestic gas demand excluding LNG and piped supply, and reform would clear delays for short laterals, interconnections and compressor upgrades needed for BTM power.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: BTM gas for data centers is a growing demand segment sensitive to small midstream approvals.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie reports BTM gas demand

insights.claim: Without reform midstream bottlenecks are likely to return, stifling upstream investment, pushing regional gas and power prices higher (most acutely in the Northeast), and slowing data center development.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Warrier, research analyst, North American power, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Failure of reform is a bullish risk for Northeast gas and power prices and a bearish one for upstream capex and data center timelines.
insights.quote: Without reform, midstream bottlenecks are likely to return, stifling upstream investment and pushing regional gas and power prices higher

insights.claim: Congestion costs exceed $10 billion a year and high-voltage line completions in the 2020s are running at under half the 2010s rate, making grid build-out urgent.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Transmission scarcity supports congestion values and grid equipment demand.

insights.claim: The next legislative frontier after permitting is inter-zonal cost allocation, i.e. who pays for lines crossing multiple utility territories and benefiting multiple states.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Cost allocation, not siting alone, will determine whether big lines get built.

insights.claim: The Restoring Renewable Energy Parity Act would require the Defense Department to sign mitigation agreements for pending wind, solar and transmission projects and overturn executive actions targeting renewables.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A possible path to unlock stalled renewable projects blocked by defense reviews.
insights.locator: The Restoring Renewable Energy Parity Act

insights.claim: Wind carries added risk because the president has targeted it directly and the federal government controls offshore leasing; its best bet is inclusion in a national multi-technology bill with congressional oversight of implementation.
insights.speaker: Siddhant Warrier, research analyst, North American power, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Wind relief depends on being bundled with other technologies; standalone wind relief is unlikely.
insights.quote: The wind industry's best bet for permitting reform is to be included in a national bill across multiple technologies and to have Congress monitor implementation

themes.theme: State policy and Texas data centers

insights.claim: If federal policy stalls under divided government, state energy policy and market rules gain importance since states hold broad authority over retail electricity, utility regulation and siting.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: State-level regulation will be the main driver of local energy and data center outcomes.

insights.claim: Gina Hinojosa's election as Texas Governor marks a significant shift in data center policy and could raise execution risk for developers with longer permitting and community approval timelines if her platform becomes law in the January 2027 session.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Texas data center developers face higher regulatory risk from early 2027.

insights.claim: Texas should remain a leading data center market given renewable resources, gas infrastructure and regulatory autonomy from FERC, but the new Governor will push constraints on speed to power.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Texas stays attractive but at a possibly slower, costlier pace of interconnection.
insights.locator: Texas will remain a leading market

insights.claim: An August executive order restricting bulk-power equipment from 24 countries including China adds uncertainty; implementation rules due in late December will clarify exposure for grid-connected data centers.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Late-December rules are a near-term catalyst for grid and data center equipment procurement.

insights.claim: New restrictive policies under the order could worsen existing supply deficits of 18% for power transformers and 14% for substation transformers.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Transformer shortages are a binding constraint, favoring domestic or non-restricted suppliers.
insights.locator: New restrictive policies under the order

insights.claim: Brown warns that economic headwinds could cause divergence, with Congress focused on affordability and the Executive pursuing foreign policy agendas, producing policy confusion and stagnation; entrenched partisanship could fuel stagnation and regulatory confusion.
insights.speaker: David Brown, Director, global integrated energy research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Policy execution risk is a key downside to the reform thesis.
insights.quote: Entrenched partisanship could fuel policy stagnation and regulatory confusion.
insights.locator: While we see the likelihood for permitting reform

insights.claim: Brown draws a precedent from 2007: Democrats took Congress during an unpopular US-led Middle East war and gridlock followed, yet the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 passed with bipartisan support (higher CAFE standards, efficiency standards, renewable fuels), and a similar effort is needed now to build affordable energy and keep US AI leadership.
insights.speaker: David Brown, Director, global integrated energy research, Wood Mackenzie
entities: Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007
insights.so_what: Historical analogue suggests bipartisan energy legislation can succeed despite gridlock, and links energy policy to AI competitiveness.
insights.locator: The US has had moments of bipartisanship
